h1: A ten minute daily taste panel for a small brewpub team
title: A Ten Minute Daily Brewpub Taste Panel | Craft Beer School
desc: Set up a ten minute daily taste panel in a small brewpub: who tastes, what, when, the form to use and how to act on the results.
teaser: Every brewpub has someone who tastes the beer. Very few have a panel. Ten minutes a day changes that.
standfirst: A small brewpub does not need a lab or a sensory room to catch faults before customers do. It needs the same few people tasting the same beers at the same time every day, writing it down and acting on what they find.
sections:
The biggest sensory failures in small breweries are not about skill. They are about habit. The head brewer tastes when there is time, the bar staff never do and nobody writes anything down. A fault creeps in over a week and the first warning is a customer sending a pint back.

A short daily panel fixes that. Ten minutes, before service, every day. It will not replace a proper sensory panel programme, but it catches most problems early and costs almost nothing.

Pick three to five people. In a typical brewpub that might be the head brewer, the assistant brewer, the bar manager and one or two senior servers. Include front-of-house staff on purpose. They pour the beer and talk to customers. They often notice changes first.

Keep the panel the same day to day where you can. Consistency matters more than expertise. Anyone on medication that affects taste, with a cold or who does not drink alcohol should feel free to sit out or to spit. Sampling is always voluntary.

Taste every beer on tap, plus any tank due for transfer or packaging that day. Pour 30 to 50 ml per person into small clear glasses. Do it at the same time each day, ideally mid-morning before service, when palates are fresh and nobody has eaten a heavy meal or drunk coffee in the last half hour.

Serve each beer at its normal dispense temperature, then let it warm for a minute before the final sniff. Faults like diacetyl and DMS show more clearly as the beer warms.

Keep it to one line per beer. A clipboard sheet or a shared spreadsheet on a tablet both work. Columns:

  1. Beer and tank or keg number
  2. True to brand: yes or no
  3. Aroma: OK, or the fault word
  4. Flavour: OK, or the fault word
  5. Appearance and foam: OK, or note
  6. Initials

True to brand is the key question. Does this beer taste the way it should, today? That is easier to answer than a score. It is the question a customer is unconsciously asking.

Agree a short fault list the team uses every time: diacetyl (butter), DMS (sweetcorn), acetaldehyde (green apple), oxidised (cardboard), sour, sulphur, phenolic (plastic or clove), metallic. Common words make results comparable.

Words only help if everyone means the same thing by them. Once a month, run a short training session with spiked samples. Commercial spiking kits let you add a known fault to a neutral lager so the team can learn diacetyl or acetaldehyde on purpose.

Now and then, add a hidden test to the daily panel. Pour the same beer twice under different codes, or run a quick triangle test when you change a recipe or supplier. It tells you who is reliable and keeps everyone sharp.

A panel that never changes anything is a ritual. Agree rules in advance:

  • If two or more tasters mark a beer not true to brand, the head brewer re-tastes before service.
  • If a fault is confirmed, pull the beer or hold the tank and note what you did.
  • Check the line, the keg and the tank before blaming the recipe. A dirty draught line can give a sour or buttery note to perfectly good beer.
  • Review the sheets weekly. Patterns matter more than single days.

Link the panel to your other quality checks, such as gravity, pH and dissolved oxygen. Our guide to a brewery QC lab on a budget covers the instruments worth buying.

Put the panel on the opening checklist with a fixed time. Keep glasses, water, crackers and spit cups in one place so setup takes a minute. Thank people for flagging problems, even false alarms. If staff fear blame, they stop reporting.

In Indian brewpubs, where heat, power cuts and cold chain hiccups can change a beer quickly, a daily check matters even more. A glycol failure overnight can push a lager warm enough to wake up diacetyl. The panel is often the first to notice.
faqs: How many people do I need for a daily taste panel?
Three to five is enough for a small brewpub. Keep the same people where possible so results are consistent.
Mainly whether the beer is true to brand. Then use a short agreed list of fault words such as diacetyl, DMS, oxidised and sour.
Do tasters have to drink the beer?
No. Small samples can be spat out. Tasting should always be voluntary. Non-drinkers can still judge aroma and appearance.
How do I train the panel?
Use spiked samples once a month so everyone learns the same faults. Add occasional hidden duplicates or triangle tests.
